records.name: Texas
records.current_summary: The facility ban (SB 8, the 'Texas Women's Privacy Act', effective 4 Dec 2025) is  actually enforced : within 48 hours (6 Dec 2025), DPS troopers checked IDs at women's restrooms in the Capitol and issued criminal-trespass warnings to four trans women, banning them from the Capitol for a year; the Attorney General opened the first state bathroom-law enforcement inquiry against Austin ISD (Mar 2026) and escalated it with a second records demand (27 Apr 2026), and a North Texas graduate student was formally 'investigated' under the law (Feb 2026). Highest absolute toll of killings of trans women in the country (44 recorded 2008–2025; 7.6 per 100k/yr); 66 anti-LGBTQ incidents in 2025 (3rd-highest US total). Rated 'Do Not Travel' — the harshest tier — in the July 2026 legal-risk assessment. Well below the national score 0.36.

sources.claim: Reports the first week of enforcement of SB 8 (Women's Privacy Act, in effect 4 Dec 2025): opponents' test of the law met with ID checks at women's restrooms in the Capitol, while the Austin City Council moved to circumvent the law's intent; colleges and cities implement divergent policies and questions remain about how the law can be enforced.

Attorney General Paxton escalated his inquiry into Austin ISD (27 Apr 2026) with a second records demand over allegations a student used a bathroom inconsistent with their sex assigned at birth, after a March investigation opened via a state tip-line complaint alleging an SB 8 violation — the first state 'bathroom law' enforcement inquiry of its kind.

State-by-state Trans Murder Monitoring analysis (2008–2025, US 428 recorded victims, 90% trans women): Texas carries the largest state count (44 recorded killings; 7.6 per 100k trans women/yr) alongside the worst-law group generally, with all rates framed as undercount floors.

July 2026 edition of the widely cited Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map: Idaho becomes the fourth-ever 'Do Not Travel' state (bathroom usage can lead to 5-year prison sentences); the adult-risk tiering places Texas and Florida among 'Do Not Travel' and South Carolina at 'Worst Laws Passed', with methodology based on law-by-law expert assessment.

records.name: Tennessee
records.current_summary: The only state with a standing  criminal ban on gender-expressive performance : the Adult Entertainment Act (2023) criminalises 'adult cabaret entertainment' — defined to include 'male or female impersonators' — on public property or anywhere a child could see it; first offence a Class A misdemeanour (up to ~11 months, $2,500 fine), repeat offences a felony (1–6 years). It is enforceable: the 6th Circuit reversed a lower-court invalidation on standing grounds (July 2024) and the Supreme Court declined review (Feb 2025) — the constitutional vagueness question has never been decided on the merits, a separate ACLU-backed suit over a DA's threat to prosecute a 2023 Pride event is ongoing, and no public prosecutions have been reported, so it reaches a visitor presenting in drag as a live charging risk rather than a nullity. A 2019 amendment widened the indecent-exposure statute; 7.8 killings per 100k trans women/yr, above the general US homicide rate. Below the national score 0.36.

sources.claim: Legal explainer of Tennessee's Adult Entertainment Act (SB 3/HB 9, 2023): defines 'adult cabaret entertainment' (incl. 'male or female impersonators', 'harmful to minors' standard), penalty ladder (Class A misdemeanour first offence up to 11 months 29 days / $2,500; Class E felony on repeat, 1–6 years / $3,000); procedural history — district court struck it down, the 6th Circuit reversed on standing without reaching the First Amendment merits, SCOTUS denied review Feb 2025; notes no publicly reported prosecutions and that the vagueness challenge remains untested.

Reports (26 Feb 2025) the U.S. Supreme Court's refusal to hear Friends of George's v. Mulroy, leaving the appeals-court dismissal in place and the Adult Entertainment Act enforceable; notes a separate ACLU suit on behalf of Blount County Pride remains ongoing after a district attorney general threatened prosecutions over a 2023 Pride festival.

State-by-state Trans Murder Monitoring analysis (2008–2025): Tennessee's rate of killings of trans women is 7.8 per 100k/yr — above the general national homicide rate (~6.0) — with all state rates framed as undercount floors that do not sort by legislative-risk category.

freshness.fact: Drag-act SCOTUS litigation upheld the law; 2025-06-18 Skrmetti upheld minor-care ban; 2026 'Riley Gaines Act' adds birth-sex placement in prisons (and shelter ban) - facility claims current and expanding.

records.name: Kansas
records.current_summary: SB 244 (enacted 18 Feb 2026 over Governor Kelly's veto) confines trans people to birth-sex facilities in government buildings and creates a private right of action allowing anyone to sue a person they suspect of violating it for ~$1,000 in damages — a bounty-hunter mechanism that exposes visitors directly; the law also invalidates Kansas-issued IDs with corrected markers (existing licences void from 26 Feb 2026, no grace period, holders notified in writing) and bars future updates. The first state flagged 'Do Not Travel' in the assessment's harshest tier this cycle; two trans men sued within days citing fear of violence. Below the national score 0.36.

sources.claim: ACLU of Kansas FAQ on SB 244 (27 Feb 2026): prohibits trans people from updating gender markers on Kansas driver's licences/state IDs and invalidates existing Kansas-issued documents reflecting a gender different from sex at birth — void as of 26 Feb 2026 with no grace period, with the Department of Revenue required to notify affected holders; explains facility-use restrictions, penalties and the out-of-state-ID position.

July 2026 edition of the anti-trans national legal-risk assessment map: Kansas remains in the top 'Do Not Travel' tier (with Florida, Texas and now Idaho); documents its bathroom-ban-plus-private-suit design as among the harshest instruments affecting interstate travel.

Feb 2026 edition: Kansas becomes the cycle's first 'Do Not Travel' state 'after enacting a bounty-style law that allows private individuals to sue transgender people encountered in restrooms for substantial amounts of money… could meaningfully affect interstate travel'; also elevates Arkansas and Indiana, and — for international visitors — designates the whole country 'Do Not Travel' absent legal-environment understanding, citing visa-revocation and detention risk.
